newsitem.title: FRANCE: FIGURE SKATING-FINNISH JUDGE AFFECTS MEN'S RESULT.
newsitem.headline: FIGURE SKATING-FINNISH JUDGE AFFECTS MEN'S RESULT.

text.p: The victory of Olympic champion Alexei Urmanov in the European men's figure skating final on Thursday came about because of controversial scoring by a Finnish judge, it became clear on Friday.
Pekka Leskinen's judging also cost Ukrainian Viacheslav Zagorodniuk a successful defence of the title.
Leskinen, a former Finnish champion, rated the last skater on the programme, Latvian-born Andrei Vlascenko of Germany, first in the free skating.
No other member of the eight-judge panel had him higher than fourth and seven judges ranked him fifth, sixth or seventh.
Urmanov, sixth after the short programme on Wednesday, rose to the top only after the marks for Vlascenko entered the computer.
Before Vlascenko skated, Urmanov was second behind Zagorodniuk with fellow Russian and former champion Ilya Kulik third and Frenchman Philippe Candeloro fourth.

After Vlascenko, Urmanov rose to first place, Candeloro advanced two positions to second, Zagorodniuk dropped two places to third and Kulik fell to fourth. Vlascenko, third after the short programme, finished sixth.
The judging of Leskinen, who as a competitor finished ninth in the 1976 Olympics and fifth in Europe the following year, was way out line with his colleagues and brought about the result.

Because of his generous assessment of Vlascenko, who had a heavy fall and other mistakes in his routine, the other contenders were a position lower in Leskinen's free-skating order of merit than they would otherwise have been.
That served to mix up the order which had existed before Vlascenko skated even though he had Urmanov, Candeloro and Zagorodniuk second, third and fourth.

Urmanov, 23, was a clear winner of the free skating with eight first-place votes. Yet that would not have been enough for overall victory had Leskinen not marked Zagorodniuk down to fourth in the free skating.
If Zagorodniuk had been one place higher in Leskinen's assessment, he would have had the gold medal with Urmanov second.

Obervers at the championship felt that the traditionally warm relationship between Finland and Latvia might have affected Leskinen's assessment in a sport in which political ties still play a significant part in the judging.
Leskinen's mysterious marking was also evident lower down the rank. He had Vakhtang Murvanidze of Georgia ninth in the free skating. No other judge had him higher than 17th and two rated him 22nd.

The event was reminiscent of the 1994 Europeans in which Jayne Torville and Christopher Dean of Britain, third before the final skaters, were boosted to first because of the scores given to the last couple, current champions Oksana Gritschuk and Evgeny Platov.
Urmanov could hardly believe his victory, his first in an international championship since his surprising triumph in the 1994 Lillehammer Olympics.
Candeloro, meanwhile, threatened to quit the sport after his marks were lower than hoped for. He relented after the final result.
